notes.definition: A lens forms an image by refracting light. A convex (converging) lens brings parallel rays to a focus at the principal focus; a concave (diverging) lens makes parallel rays spread out as if they came from the principal focus. The distance from the lens to the principal focus is the focal length. Magnification = image height ÷ object height.
explanation: A lens is a shaped piece of transparent material, such as glass or plastic, that refracts light to form an image. A convex lens is thicker in the middle than at the edges. Rays of light parallel to the principal axis are refracted and brought together (converge) at a point called the principal focus. A concave lens is thinner in the middle. It makes parallel rays spread out (diverge) so that they appear to come from a principal focus on the same side of the lens as the light arrives. Each lens has a principal focus on each side. The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus is the focal length.

In ray diagrams, lenses are drawn using symbols. A convex lens is a vertical line with outward-pointing arrowheads at each end; a concave lens is a vertical line with inward-pointing arrowheads at each end. The principal axis is a horizontal line through the centre of the lens, and F marks the principal focus on each side. To find the image of the top of an object, draw two rays: one parallel to the principal axis, which is refracted through F (convex lens) or away from the lens as if it came from F (concave lens); and one through the centre of the lens, which passes straight through without changing direction. Where the rays meet (or appear to meet) is the top of the image.

An image is real if the light rays actually meet there; a real image can be projected onto a screen. An image is virtual if the rays only appear to come from it; it cannot be projected onto a screen and you see it by looking through the lens. The image from a convex lens can be real or virtual. If the object is further from the lens than F, the image is real and inverted (upside down) on the other side of the lens; beyond 2F the image is diminished, and between F and 2F it is magnified. If the object is closer to the lens than F, the image is virtual, upright and magnified: this is how a magnifying glass works. The image produced by a concave lens is always virtual, upright and diminished.

The magnification produced by a lens is calculated using magnification = image height ÷ object height. This equation is given on the Physics equation sheet, but you must be able to use and rearrange it. Magnification is a ratio, so it has no units, but the image height and object height must be measured in the same unit, either mm or cm. A magnification greater than 1 means the image is bigger than the object; less than 1 means it is smaller. Rearranged, image height = magnification × object height, and object height = image height ÷ magnification.

Lenses are used in cameras, projectors, spectacles and magnifying glasses. A camera uses a convex lens to form a real, inverted, diminished image on the sensor. Spectacles for short sight use concave lenses, and for long sight use convex lenses. The more curved the surfaces of a lens, the more strongly it refracts light and the shorter its focal length.
keyFacts: A lens forms an image by refracting light.
Convex lens: parallel rays converge to the principal focus.
Concave lens: parallel rays diverge as if from the principal focus.
Focal length: distance from the lens to the principal focus.
Convex symbol: line with outward arrowheads; concave symbol: line with inward arrowheads.
A ray through the centre of a lens is not deviated.
Real image: rays actually meet; can be projected on a screen.
Virtual image: rays only appear to meet; cannot be projected.
Convex lens images can be real or virtual; concave lens images are always virtual.
magnification = image height ÷ object height (no units; same units for both heights).

keyTerms.definition: A lens that is thicker in the middle and brings parallel rays of light together at the principal focus.
A lens that is thinner in the middle and spreads parallel rays out as if they came from the principal focus.
The point where rays parallel to the principal axis meet (convex) or appear to come from (concave) after passing through the lens.
The distance from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.
The line through the centre of a lens at right angles to it.
An image formed where light rays actually meet; it can be projected onto a screen.
An image from which light rays only appear to come; it cannot be projected onto a screen.
The ratio of image height to object height.

equations.name: Magnification
equations.units: no units (a ratio); both heights in the same unit, mm or cm

workedExamples.title: Calculating magnification
workedExamples.question: A magnifying glass forms an image 6.0 cm tall of an insect 2.0 cm tall. Calculate the magnification.

workedExamples.title: Mixed units
workedExamples.question: An object 1.5 cm tall produces an image 45 mm tall. Calculate the magnification.
steps: Put both heights in the same unit: 45 mm = 4.5 cm.

workedExamples.title: Rearranging to find the object height
workedExamples.question: A camera lens produces an image 2.4 cm tall with a magnification of 0.50. Calculate the height of the object.
steps: Rearrange: object height = image height ÷ magnification.

workedExamples.title: Describing an image from a ray diagram
workedExamples.question: A ray diagram for a convex lens shows the image formed on the opposite side of the lens, upside down and smaller than the object. Describe the image fully.
steps: The rays actually meet on the other side of the lens, so the image is real.
It is smaller than the object: diminished.
workedExamples.answer: Real, inverted and diminished (the object is beyond 2F).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think magnification has units such as cm.
misconceptions.right: In fact it is a ratio of two heights in the same unit, so it has no units.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a virtual image is not really there and cannot be seen.
misconceptions.right: In fact you can see a virtual image by looking through the lens, but it cannot be projected onto a screen.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think a convex lens always magnifies.
misconceptions.right: In fact an object beyond 2F gives a diminished image; it only magnifies when the object is between F and 2F (real) or inside F (virtual).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think concave lenses can form real images of real objects.
misconceptions.right: In fact the image formed by a concave lens is always virtual.

realWorld: Cameras and the human eye use convex lenses to form real, inverted images on a sensor or the retina.
Magnifying glasses use a convex lens with the object inside the focal length to give a virtual, magnified image.
Glasses for short-sighted people use concave lenses; for long-sighted people, convex lenses.
Projectors use a convex lens to produce a real, magnified image on a screen.
separateOnlyContent: This whole subtopic (lenses, ray diagrams, real and virtual images, magnification) is in separate Physics only.
examTips: Use a ruler and draw two rays from the top of the object: one parallel to the axis and one through the centre of the lens. Add arrows.
For virtual images, extend the rays backwards with dashed lines to find where they appear to come from.
Describe an image with three words: real or virtual, upright or inverted, magnified or diminished.
Magnification has no units; convert both heights to the same unit (mm or cm) first.
Learn the symbols: convex has arrowheads pointing outwards, concave has arrowheads pointing inwards.
summary: Convex lenses converge parallel rays at the principal focus; concave lenses diverge them.
Focal length is the distance from the lens to the principal focus.
Convex lens images can be real or virtual; concave lens images are always virtual.
Real images can be projected; virtual images cannot.
magnification = image height ÷ object height (no units).

questions.question: How does a lens form an image?
markScheme: 1 mark: By refracting light
questions.explanation: Lenses change the direction of light by refraction as it passes through.

questions.question: What is meant by the focal length of a lens?
options: The distance from the lens to the principal focus
The distance from the object to the image
markScheme: 1 mark: The distance from the lens to the principal focus
questions.explanation: Focal length is measured from the centre of the lens to the principal focus.

questions.question: Which equation links image height, object height and magnification?
markScheme: 1 mark: magnification = image height ÷ object height
questions.explanation: Magnification is image height divided by object height.

questions.question: What type of image is always produced by a concave lens?
markScheme: 1 mark: Virtual
questions.explanation: A concave lens always forms a virtual, upright, diminished image.

questions.question: Which statement describes a real image?
options: It can only be seen by looking into the lens
It is formed where light rays actually meet and can be projected onto a screen
markScheme: 1 mark: It is formed where light rays actually meet and can be projected onto a screen
questions.explanation: Real images are where rays truly meet, so a screen placed there shows the image. Virtual images cannot be projected.

markScheme: 1 mark: image height = 6.0 cm and object height = 2.0 cm, so magnification = 6.0 ÷ 2.0
1 mark: 3.0
questions.explanation: From the grid, the object is 2 squares (2.0 cm) tall and the virtual image is 6 squares (6.0 cm) tall. magnification = image height ÷ object height = 6.0 ÷ 2.0 = 3.0. Magnification has no unit. Dividing the other way gives 0.33, which would mean the image is smaller than the object.

questions.question:
A camera lens produces an image 1.5 cm tall of an object 6.0 cm tall.
Calculate the magnification.
Use the equation:
magnification = image height ÷ object height
markScheme: 1 mark: 0.25
questions.explanation: 1.5 ÷ 6.0 = 0.25. The image is a quarter of the size of the object.

questions.question:
A lens produces a magnification of 4.0.
The object is 3.0 mm tall.
Calculate the height of the image.
Use the equation:
magnification = image height ÷ object height
markScheme: 1 mark: image height = 4.0 × 3.0
1 mark: 12 mm
questions.explanation: Rearranging, image height = magnification × object height = 4.0 × 3.0 = 12 mm.

questions.question:
A lens produces an image 2.4 cm tall.
The magnification is 0.50.
Calculate the height of the object.
Use the equation:
magnification = image height ÷ object height
markScheme: 1 mark: object height = 2.4 ÷ 0.50
1 mark: 4.8 cm
questions.explanation: object height = image height ÷ magnification = 2.4 ÷ 0.50 = 4.8 cm.

questions.question:
An object 1.5 cm tall forms an image 45 mm tall.
Calculate the magnification.
Use the equation:
magnification = image height ÷ object height
markScheme: 1 mark: 45 mm = 4.5 cm (or 1.5 cm = 15 mm)
1 mark: 3.0
questions.explanation: Both heights must be in the same unit: 45 ÷ 15 = 3.0. Dividing 45 by 1.5 gives 30, a common error.

questions.question:
An object 0.80 cm tall produces an image 2.0 cm tall.
Calculate the magnification.
Use the equation:
magnification = image height ÷ object height
markScheme: 1 mark: 2.5
questions.explanation: magnification = 2.0 ÷ 0.80 = 2.5.

questions.question:
A magnifying glass produces a magnification of 5.0.
The image of a printed letter is 2.5 cm tall.
Calculate the height of the printed letter in millimetres.
Use the equation:
magnification = image height ÷ object height
markScheme: 1 mark: object height = 2.5 ÷ 5.0
1 mark: = 0.50 cm
1 mark: = 5.0 mm
questions.explanation: object height = 2.5 ÷ 5.0 = 0.50 cm = 5.0 mm.

questions.question: What is meant by the principal focus of a convex lens?
acceptedAnswers: rays parallel to axis brought to a focus
markScheme: 1 mark: the point where rays parallel to the principal axis are brought together (focused) after passing through the lens
questions.explanation: For a concave lens, it is the point the refracted rays appear to come from.

questions.question: Explain the difference between a real image and a virtual image.
acceptedAnswers: virtual rays appear to come from
markScheme: 1 mark: a real image is where light rays actually meet / can be projected onto a screen
1 mark: a virtual image is where rays only appear to come from / cannot be projected onto a screen
questions.explanation: This is why a projector (real image) can show a picture on a wall but a magnifying glass (virtual) cannot.

Compare what happens to the rays when they pass through each lens.

1 mark: concave: rays diverge / spread out as if from the principal focus
questions.explanation: A comparison needs a point about each lens.

questions.question:
A convex lens is used as a magnifying glass.
The lens is closer to the object than its focal length.
Describe the image formed.
markScheme: 1 mark: virtual
1 mark: upright
1 mark: magnified
questions.explanation: Each of the three words earns a mark.

questions.question:
A student makes this statement.
'The magnification of the lens is 3 cm.'
Explain what is wrong with the statement.
markScheme: 1 mark: magnification has no units
1 mark: because it is a ratio of two heights measured in the same unit, so the units cancel
questions.explanation: Magnification should be written as a number only, for example 3.

markScheme: Indicative content:
draw the principal axis and the convex lens symbol; mark F and 2F on both sides
draw the object as an upright arrow on the axis beyond 2F
draw a ray from the top of the object parallel to the axis to the lens, then refracted through F on the other side
draw a ray from the top of the object through the centre of the lens, undeviated
where the two rays cross is the top of the image
image is real, inverted and diminished, between F and 2F
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): both construction rays correctly described and image located and described.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one ray described or image described without construction.
questions.explanation: Two rays are enough to locate an image: parallel then through F, and straight through the centre.

questions.question:
Compare the images that can be formed by convex lenses and concave lenses.
Your answer should include how ray diagrams are used to find each image and the types of image produced.
markScheme: Indicative content:
both lenses refract light to form images; symbols differ (outward vs inward arrowheads)
convex: parallel rays converge to the principal focus; concave: parallel rays diverge as if from the principal focus
ray through centre is undeviated for both
convex: parallel ray refracted through F on far side; concave: parallel ray refracted away, traced back (dashed) to F on near side
convex, object beyond F: real, inverted image; beyond 2F diminished, between F and 2F magnified
convex, object inside F: virtual, upright, magnified (magnifying glass)
concave: always virtual, upright, diminished
real images can be projected, virtual cannot
magnification = image height ÷ object height
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed comparison covering ray construction and image types for both lenses, including real and virtual.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): some comparison of ray behaviour and image types.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about one or both lenses.
questions.explanation: Good answers contrast converging and diverging, and the real/virtual nature of images for each lens.

questions.question:
A lens produces a magnification of 6.0.
The image is 18 mm tall.
Calculate the height of the object.
Use the equation:
magnification = image height ÷ object height
markScheme: 1 mark: object height = 18 ÷ 6.0
1 mark: 3.0 mm
questions.explanation: object height = image height ÷ magnification = 18 ÷ 6.0 = 3.0 mm.

questions.question: Name the type of lens used in a magnifying glass.
markScheme: 1 mark: convex (converging) lens
questions.explanation: Only a convex lens can produce a magnified image; a concave lens always gives a diminished image.
